title: Level 7: Fast PWM — LED Fading with Timer0
aim: To use Timer0 in Fast PWM mode on the ATmega328P to generate a hardware PWM signal on OC0A (PD6 / Pin 6), smoothly fading an LED brightness from 0% to 100% and back using OCR0A.
objective: Understand Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) fundamentals, Fast PWM waveform generation registers (TCCR0A, TCCR0B, OCR0A), the non-inverting/inverting OC0A output modes, and how duty cycle maps to perceived LED brightness.
theory:
What is PWM?

Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) is a technique for simulating an analog voltage level using a digital signal that rapidly alternates between HIGH and LOW. The average voltage delivered to a load depends on the ratio of time spent HIGH vs. LOW in each cycle. This ratio is called the duty cycle.

Duty Cycle = (ON time / Total Period) × 100%
V_avg = V_high × Duty Cycle

At 5 V supply: 25% duty cycle → 1.25 V average, 50% → 2.5 V, 100% → 5 V. An LED perceives this average voltage and lights proportionally (with some gamma correction).

Fast PWM Mode (Mode 3)

In Fast PWM mode, TCNT0 counts from 0 up to 255 (TOP = 0xFF), then immediately resets to 0 and begins again — a single-slope upward ramp. This produces the highest PWM frequency possible for a given prescaler. The compare register OCR0A sets the duty cycle:

  • When TCNT0 = 0 → output pin (OC0A) goes HIGH
  • When TCNT0 = OCR0A → output pin goes LOW
  • Result: duty cycle = OCR0A / 256 × 100%

Setting OCR0A = 0 gives 0% duty (always LOW). Setting OCR0A = 255 gives ~100% duty (always HIGH). Setting OCR0A = 128 gives 50% (2.5 V average).

TCCR0A — Waveform Generation & Compare Output

  • WGM01:WGM00 = 1:1 — Selects Fast PWM Mode 3 (TOP = 0xFF)
  • COM0A1:COM0A0 = 1:0 — Non-inverting mode: OC0A goes HIGH on BOTTOM, LOW on OCR0A match. This is the standard fade direction.

Combined: TCCR0A = (1<<COM0A1) | (1<<WGM01) | (1<<WGM00);

TCCR0B — Prescaler

The PWM frequency is determined by the prescaler:
f_PWM = F_CPU / (prescaler × 256)
At 16 MHz ÷8: f_PWM = 16M / (8 × 256) = 7,812 Hz — above the flicker threshold. The LED appears to fade smoothly.

OCR0A — The Duty Cycle Register

Writing any value 0–255 to OCR0A changes the duty cycle in real time. No ISR needed — simply increment/decrement OCR0A in the main loop with a short delay to create a fade effect. The timer peripheral automatically generates the correct waveform.

OC0A Pin — PD6 (Arduino Pin 6)

The hardware PWM output is only available on the dedicated OC0A pin (PD6). For PWM to work, PD6 must be configured as output (DDRD bit 6 = 1) — the timer hardware takes over pin control when non-inverting mode is enabled.

pretest.question: What does 'duty cycle' mean in PWM?
options: The frequency of the PWM signal
The ratio of HIGH time to total period, expressed as a percentage
pretest.explanation: Duty cycle = (ON time / Period) × 100%. It determines the average output voltage and thus LED brightness or motor speed.

pretest.question: What is the average output voltage at 5 V with 75% duty cycle PWM?
In Fast PWM Mode 3, what is the TOP value of TCNT0?
pretest.explanation: In Fast PWM Mode 3 (WGM01=1, WGM00=1, WGM02=0), the TOP is fixed at 0xFF = 255. TCNT0 counts 0→255 then resets.

pretest.question: How do you select Fast PWM mode in TCCR0A?
pretest.explanation: WGM01=1, WGM00=1 in TCCR0A (combined with WGM02=0 in TCCR0B) selects Fast PWM Mode 3 with TOP = 0xFF.

pretest.question: What does COM0A1:COM0A0 = 1:0 in TCCR0A configure?
options: Non-inverting PWM — OC0A set at BOTTOM, cleared at OCR0A match
pretest.explanation: COM0A1=1, COM0A0=0 enables non-inverting Fast PWM on OC0A: pin goes HIGH at count 0, LOW when count reaches OCR0A.

pretest.question: Which physical pin is OC0A on the ATmega328P / Arduino Uno?
pretest.explanation: OC0A is mapped to PD6 (Port D, bit 6), which is Arduino Uno Digital Pin 6. PD5 is OC0B, PB1 is OC1A.

pretest.question: At 16 MHz with ÷8 prescaler in Fast PWM, what is the PWM frequency?
pretest.explanation: f_PWM = F_CPU / (prescaler × 256) = 16,000,000 / (8 × 256) = 7,812 Hz. This is well above the 100 Hz flicker threshold.

pretest.question: What OCR0A value produces a 50% duty cycle?
Why must PD6 be configured as output (DDRD bit 6 = 1) for hardware PWM?
options: Timer needs to read the pin
The timer hardware drives the pin — it must be in output mode
pretest.explanation: In hardware PWM, the timer peripheral drives the OC0A pin directly. If DDR is not set to output, the pin stays Hi-Z regardless of timer configuration.

pretest.question: What header file provides _delay_ms() for the fade delay?
pretest.explanation: <util/delay.h> provides _delay_ms(). F_CPU must be defined before including it.

procedure: Include headers: #include <avr/io.h> and #include <util/delay.h>. Define #define F_CPU 16000000UL. Wire the LED (with 330 Ω resistor) to Pin 6 (PD6 = OC0A).
Configure OC0A pin as output: DDRD |= (1 << PD6);. The timer will take over pin control, but the DDR must be set to output for the hardware to drive the pin.

Configure Timer0 for Fast PWM Mode 3 with non-inverting output on OC0A. Write to TCCR0A: TCCR0A = (1 << COM0A1) | (1 << WGM01) | (1 << WGM00);. This sets non-inverting mode (COM0A1=1, COM0A0=0) and Fast PWM (WGM01=1, WGM00=1).
Set the prescaler to ÷8 in TCCR0B to get a 7.8 kHz PWM frequency — this is smooth and flicker-free: TCCR0B = (1 << CS01);. This starts the timer. WGM02 remains 0, keeping TOP = 255.
Set the initial duty cycle to 0 by writing 0 to OCR0A: OCR0A = 0;. The LED is off initially.

In the main loop, create a fade-up effect: loop from 0 to 255, incrementing OCR0A by 1 each iteration with a short delay: for(uint8_t i = 0; i < 255; i++) { OCR0A = i; _delay_ms(5); }. Over 255 × 5 ms = 1.275 seconds the LED fades from off to full brightness.
Create a fade-down effect immediately after: for(uint8_t i = 255; i > 0; i--) { OCR0A = i; _delay_ms(5); }. The LED smoothly dims from full to off.

Wrap both fade loops in the infinite while(1) to create a continuous breathing/pulsing effect. Observe that the LED fades smoothly — no stutter — because the PWM waveform is generated entirely in hardware.

posttest.question: What OCR0A value gives 25% duty cycle (very dim LED)?
What is the PWM frequency at 16 MHz with ÷64 prescaler in Fast PWM mode?
posttest.explanation: f_PWM = 16,000,000 / (64 × 256) = 976 Hz. Still above the flicker threshold, but decreasing resolution of the fade steps.

posttest.question: What happens if OCR0A = 0 in non-inverting Fast PWM?
posttest.explanation: At OCR0A=0, the compare happens at the very bottom. In fast PWM, output is LOW the entire cycle — 0% duty, LED fully off.

posttest.question: What happens if OCR0A = 255 in non-inverting Fast PWM?
options: Almost 100% HIGH — one cycle of LOW at overflow
posttest.explanation: At OCR0A=255, the pin is set LOW at exactly the overflow point (count=255→0), giving a very brief LOW pulse. Duty is approximately 100%.

posttest.question: What is 'Phase Correct PWM' and how does it differ from Fast PWM?
options: Dual-slope counting (up then down) giving symmetric waveform, half the frequency
posttest.explanation: Phase Correct PWM counts 0→255→0 (dual-slope), producing a symmetric waveform with no phase shift — ideal for motor control. Frequency is half of Fast PWM at same prescaler.

posttest.question: Which timer peripheral pin generates OC1A output?
posttest.explanation: OC1A is mapped to PB1 (Port B, Pin 1), which is Arduino Uno Digital Pin 9. This is Timer1's Compare A output.

posttest.question: Which is NOT a valid ATmega328P port?
posttest.explanation: ATmega328P has only Port B, C, and D.

posttest.question: What happens to SRAM when power is removed?
posttest.explanation: SRAM is volatile — all data is immediately lost on power-off or reset.

posttest.question: In an ISR, interrupts are automatically:
posttest.explanation: The AVR clears the I-bit in SREG upon entering any ISR to prevent nested interrupts.

posttest.question: What does the SREG register contain?
posttest.explanation: SREG is the Status Register holding arithmetic flags (C, Z, N, V) and the global interrupt enable bit (I).

feedback: Excellent! You have generated your first hardware PWM signal and used it for analog-like LED control. Fast PWM is used in motor speed control, audio DAC output, servo positioning, and power supply regulation — essential in every product.
